rv.q: The result is an intimate epic that becomes a masterly study of acting as well as of the intricacies of high finance.
This story about the rise and tumultuous fall of the Lehman Brothers, both the family and the bank they founded, is grown-up theatre at its best.
This is a powerful, thought-provoking play and Mendes has directed it with extraordinary elegance and penetration.
It’s a cross section of the roots of capitalism, beautifully adapted, artfully staged and wonderfully acted.
This isn’t a hydra-headed, David Hare-style lesson in economic nuance but a lean three-hander in which the hubristic history of American capitalism takes on the deceptive charm of a folk tale.
'The Lehman Trilogy' is an elegantly told voyage through American history, and one that sheds plenty of light on the country's present, turbulent shape.
Ben Miles is riveting: concentrated, stealthy, authentic.
Whether the work achieves its goal, however, is a different matter.
There are moments when this politically charged saga risks feeling like a dramatised Wikipedia entry.
The Lehman Trilogy, the National Theatre premiere in which a long-established director surprises his audience and, in the process, surpasses himself.

Across three hours, and three acts, three magnificent actors conjure the story of the three Lehman brothers, the fate of whose company came to symbolise something about the state of America and of capitalism.
It's big news that movie director Sam Mendes took the helm on this one but his staging, along with Stefano Massini's play as adapted by Ben Power, though admirable is, ultimately unsatisfying.

Even against this intimidating backdrop, The Lehman Trilogy is an outstanding achievement, a hypnotic three and a half hour journey through the history of the eponymous company, and through capitalism itself.
This fascinating excursion is finally more statuesque than pressing.

cn.t: Critics hail this epic as "grown-up theatre at its best," praising Mendes' minimalist staging and three magnificent actors who chart 150 years of capitalism. Most find it astonishing and enthralling, though some cite diminishing dramatic returns.
